In [[mathematics]], an '''infinite expression''' is an [[Expression (mathematics)|expression]] in which some [[Operation (mathematics)|operators]] take an infinite number of [[Argument of a function|arguments]], or in which the nesting of the operators continues to an infinite depth.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Helmer |first1=Olaf |authorlink1=Olaf Helmer |date=January 1938 |title=The syntax of a language with infinite expressions |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |volume=44 |issue=1 |pages=33–34 |type=Abstract |issn=0002-9904 |oclc=5797393 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1938-06672-4|doi-access=free }}.</ref>  A generic concept for infinite expression can lead to ill-defined or self-inconsistent constructions (much like a [[universal set|set of all sets]]), but there are several instances of infinite expressions that are well-defined.

==Examples==
Examples of well-defined infinite expressions are<ref>
{{cite book |last1=Euler |first1=Leonhard |authorlink1=Leonhard Euler |others=J.D. Blanton (translator) |title=Introduction to Analysis of the Infinite, Book I |date=November 1, 1988 |publisher=Springer Verlag |isbn=978-0-387-96824-7 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=H58dmcLEnk4C&dq=%22continued+fraction%22+%22infinite+expression%22&pg=PA303 303] |type=Hardcover}}
</ref>

* [[infinite sum]]s, such as

:: <math>\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n = a_0 + a_1 + a_2 + \cdots \,</math>

* [[infinite product]]s, such as

:: <math>\prod_{n=0}^\infty b_n = b_0 \times b_1 \times b_2 \times \cdots </math>

* [[Nested radical#Infinitely nested radicals|infinite nested radical]]s, such as

:: <math>\sqrt{1+2\sqrt{1+3 \sqrt{1+\cdots}}} </math>

* [[Tetration#Extension_to_infinite_heights|infinite power towers]],<ref>{{cite arXiv|first=Luca|last=Moroni|year=2019|title=The strange properties of the infinite power tower|class=math.HO |eprint=1908.05559}}</ref> such as 

:: <math>\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}^{\cdot^{\cdot^{\cdot}}}}} </math>

* [[continued fraction|infinite continued fractions]], such as

:: <math>c_0 + \underset{n=1}{\overset{\infty}{\mathrm K}} \frac{1}{c_n} = c_0 + \cfrac{1}{c_1 + \cfrac{1}{c_2 + \cfrac{1}{c_3 + \cfrac{1}{c_4 + \ddots}}}},</math>
: where the left hand side uses [[Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]]'s [[generalized continued fraction|Kettenbruch notation]].<ref>
{{cite book |last1=Wall |first1=Hubert Stanley |authorlink1=Hubert Stanley Wall |title=Analytic Theory of Continued Fractions |date=March 28, 2000 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |isbn=978-0-8218-2106-0 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=eE8PpgM3ucMC&dq=%22continued+fraction%22+%22infinite+expression%22&pg=PA14 14] |type=Hardcover}}
</ref>

In [[infinitary logic]], one can use infinite [[Logical conjunction|conjunctions]] and infinite [[Logical disjunction|disjunctions]].

Even for well-defined infinite expressions, the ''value'' of the infinite expression may be ambiguous or not well-defined; for instance, there are multiple summation rules available for assigning values to series, and the same series may have different values according to different summation rules if the series is not [[absolute convergence|absolutely convergent]].
